body_markdown:
Lord March’s country estate is home the Goodwood circuit, as well as two of the greatest car events on earth—Festival of Speed, and Revival. “Always check the parking lot for cool stuff” is a car show lesson I learned at Goodwood House. I was there for the Festival of Speed when it was still a new-ish event. After ogling race cars for hours and actually getting to meet Sir Stirling Moss, I wandered out to the parking lots—I was too young to rent a car, so I’d come by train—and was rewarded with a cornucopia of Frazer-Nashes, Lancia Aurelias, and more. At the Goodwood Revival, however, the parking lot full of cool stuff vistors drove to the event is a core part of the experience.


The Revival is a time-warp smörgåsbord of cars, culture,[and fashion](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/clothes-and-cars-why-dress-the-part/) stitched together by[genuinely exciting vintage motorsport](https://www.hagerty.com/media/events/goodwood-revival-gallery-real-vintage-racing-in-theme-park-wrapping/) battles. It is also a truly immersive experience; aside from rescue equipment, post-1966 vehicles aren’t allowed inside the circuit during the event. Even the food trucks are vintage machines. But while racing and fashion get most of the glory, the “Pre-’66 and Tax Exempt parking lots” have been an attraction for decades.


At what’s now called the Revival Car Show, the classic lot sits closest to the main entrances, so many attendees walk through it going both in and out. Pre-’66 cars still get pride of place, but eventually, organizers added an outer ring in this classic lot for slightly newer (but still old) classics from the 1970s and 1980s. According to the organizers, as many as 6000 classics have been in the lot at any one time. It’s so large, and has such variety, that you could easily spend all of Revival weekend just wandering its aisles.


We’ve covered this aspect of the Revival[before](https://www.hagerty.com/media/events/public-parking-lot-at-goodwood-revival/) , but this is a parking lot where, in any given year, you might see a one-off concept car or a Bugatti that once adorned a motor show stand. So we decided to showcase ten of this year’s rarest and most interesting finds. This is by no means a comprehensive list, but without further adieu…


## 1948 Bristol 400


Alex Kwanten


Goodwood Motor Circuit first opened on September 18, 1948, and the very first car to roar around it was a Bristol 400 just like this one. Behind the wheel was “Freddie” March, the 9th Duke of Richmond, an amateur racer who created the road course (Britain’s first postwar racing venue) from a WW2 airfield. The Bristol returned when his grandson, the current Duke, used it to open the first Revival in 1998. As cars go, it was an appropriate choice.


An aircraft manufacturer looking to diversify as WW2 wound down, Bristol branched out into Gran Turismos for the connoisseur. But rather than design a car from scratch, it picked a good set of parts to make its own. First it acquired Frazer-Nash, who held the U.K. license to the pre-war BMW 328 engine, then it bought the design plans for the 326, 327 and 328, trading the plans for hard currency that would help BMW rebuild.


The Bristol 400 was a blend of the best of these elements, a 326 chassis with a potent 2.0-liter inline-six derived from the 328 engine and a wind-tunnel-honed body resembling an updated 327. Fast and luxurious, the 400[put Bristol on the map](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/exclusive-expensive-eccentric-and-expired-a-potted-history-of-bristol-cars/) as a serious carmaker, though only 487 were made before it gave way to the more modern-looking 401 and its[drop-top version, the 402](https://www.hagerty.com/media/archived/bristol-402/) . This particular car was built right around the time Goodwood opened, in September 1948.


## 1930 Austin 7 Swallow


Alex Kwanten


The most popular British car of the first half of the 20th century, the[Austin 7](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/car-profiles/the-full-english-austin-seven/) was rarely fancy, but there are some exceptions. This is an Austin 7 Swallow, an aerodynamic coupe version created by Swallow Coachbuilding, founded by William Walmsley and William Lyons as “Swallow Sidecar” in 1922. (Yes,[that William Lyons](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/joy-of-six-jaguar-e-type-blue-ridge/) .) The 7 was Swallow’s first coachbuilt car and it was immediately popular, helping generate the money that ultimately allowed the outfit to build the[SS cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/forget-the-ss-badge-this-prewar-beast-is-a-jaguar-in-soul-and-design/) that eventually became Jaguar.


Styled by Lyons and staffer Cyril Holland, the Swallow-bodied 7 is glamorous on the outside, though its pert lines make the 7’s already teensy interior even smaller. Even the doors are comically tiny. Underneath, it’s more or less a standard 7, with a 10.5-horsepower 747-cc sidevalve-four. Many 7s ended up as stripped-down racers, but the Swallow was always a cut above the regular models. Exact production figures are unknown, but probably no more than 3500 Austin 7 Swallows were built from 1928 to 1932.


## 1927 BNC 527 Sport Monza


Alex Kwanten


Chances are you’ve never even heard of BNC, but this French make was a keen rival of Amilcar and Salmson. Founded in 1922 by ex-Hispano Suiza engineer Lucien Bollack and his financier friend, René Netter, the company built hot voiturettes for road and track with engines under 1.1 liters out of a Levellois-Perret garage. An outgrowth of the cyclecar craze in France, these sports cars set the stage for later small British rivals, and they were built to win races. BNC was an early adopter of superchargers and its cars competed at Le Mans.


The company was always an extreme niche builder, but in the 1920s its cars went from strength to strength. 1927 saw the arrival of the trademark laid-back oval radiator and the 527 Monza, which used either a S.C.A.P. or Ruby engine depending on the buyer, and could be fitted with a supercharger with roughly 40 horsepower. Unfortunately 1927 was the company’s peak, as it was already having financial issues and was taken over by entrepreneur Charles de Ricou in 1928, ousting the founders. It closed in 1931. Production numbers are unknown.


## 1967 Rover 2000TCZ


Alex Kwanten


It doesn’t get any rarer than a one-of-one, and the Rover TCZ is exactly that. If its lines suggest a Lancia Fulvia Zagato to you, your eyes do not deceive you. Styled by Ercole Spada at the Italian carrozzeria, the TCZ was a Zagato-bodied concept for a[Rover P6](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/beryl-of-fun-this-isnt-your-ordinary-rover-p6/) Coupe. It debuted at the 1967 Turin motor show, and while a long, low stunner of a fastback, it was unfortunately upstaged by both the Alfa Romeo 33, Lamborghini Marzal, Fiat Dino Coupe, and the BMC-Pininfarina Aerodynamica 1800.


Underneath, the TCZ is basically a standard[P6 2000TC](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/buying-guide-rover-p6-1963-1977/) with various extra parts, like a one-off steering wheel. Gianni Zagato himself approached Rover to do the car, in hopes of keeping his production lines humming, but Rover had no need for more P6 variants and it was already working on an in-house coupe by David Bache. When the British Leyland merger happened, all hope of production ended. In 1968, Zagato sold it off and it’s been in private hands since, at one point selling for £1500 at a Worcestershire Rover dealer.


## 1933 Bugatti Type 49 Drophead by Van Risjwijk


Alex Kwanten


There were no fewer than five Bugattis in the Revival parking lot, all of them unusual, and this big Type 49 droptop was parked right next to a Type 43 Grand Sport. While most modern Bugatti fans are drawn to the sportier models, this big machine is a model of luxurious opulence. The Type 49 was the last design to use Bugatti’s original SOHC straight eight, derived from the Type 29 racer. By the time of the Type 49, it had been bored and stroked to 3.3 liters and about 85 horsepower.


It’s nowhere near as quick as the Type 43 GS, but this one’s more about style and smoothness than speed anyway, despite rolling on those amazing machined aluminum wheels. Built in Molsheim in May of 1933, the car was shipped to the Netherlands and bodied by coachbuilder Van Risjwijk in The Hague. An old-line constructor, Van Rijswijk mostly built flashy bodies for big cars—Isotta-Fraschini, Packard, Minerva and the like, and this car was showcased on its stand at the 1934 Amsterdam motor show. 470 Type 49s were made from 1930–34, but only one like this. Somebody drove it to Goodwood from Belgium.


## 1952 Aston-Martin DB2 Vantage by Graber


Alex Kwanten


All due respect to the original four-cylinder “2-Liter Sports,” retroactively the DB1, it’s the DB2 and its W.O. Bentley-designed, Lagonda-sourced inline six that anchored[the glorious David Brown era of Aston-Martins](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/a-century-of-aston-martin-at-the-petersen-automotive-museum/) . Honed at Le Mans, the tube-frame, Frank Feeley-styled DB2 debuted in New York in the spring of 1950, about three years after tractor magnate Brown had bought the flagging Aston and Lagonda companies and combined them. The[DB2](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/build-it-yourself-the-first-aston-martin-db2-could-be-yours-for-250000/) was an immediate success, and it soon became Aston’s best-selling model up to that time, but this one isn’t a normal DB2.


The first upgrade for this model, the DB2 Vantage, added larger carbs, a hotter cam, and high-compression pistons, but Aston also soon added a convertible model. This one, however, goes even further, being one of three DB2 Vantage droptops bodied by Swiss coachbuilder Graber—and the only example that survives today.


## 1983 Aston Martin Lagonda


Alex Kwanten


The small-batch nature of pre-war cars and their age means the rarest of the rare at Goodwood are always old and obscure, but there are also plenty of newer and very unusual machines in the lot. One of the most extreme of those was this Swedish-registered, vividly green 1983 Aston-Martin Lagonda. As if this[notoriously complex car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/aston-martins-outlandish-lagonda-turns-50/) didn’t have enough wiring in it already, this one comes complete with a television, a VCR and a full entertainment center in the back seat, and a very Eighties “wingding” antenna to boot.


Styled by William Towns, the wedge-shaped Lagonda was decades ahead of other luxury sedans when it debuted in 1976, but its touch-sensitive controls, talking warning systems and bevy of computers were so complex it took another three years to get it into production. Even then it was undercooked and famously unreliable, but it did look amazing and it was fast, with a 280-horse V-8. Production totaled 458 for these early Lagonda before major updates arrived in 1986.


## 1975 Daimler Double Six Coupe


Alex Kwanten


At first, you might think this is the rare Jaguar XJ6C Coupé, but you’d be wrong. This is an even-rarer[Daimler Double Six Coupé](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/automotive-history/the-jaguar-xj12-and-daimler-double-six-remembered/) , one of the last flourishes of the fading Daimler brand. Production of the two-door XJ models lasted from the spring of 1975 to the fall of 1978, a period that coincided with the absolute nadir of Jaguar quality control and the height of British Leyland’s labor troubles. It was a gorgeous design, but when it came time to prioritize a two-door during an era of cutbacks, the XJS was always going to win.


Daimler was a shadow of its former self by the time this car was built in December of ‘75, but it persisted as a rebadged Jag for a long time after. In the mid-1970s, however, and with memories of OPEC I still fresh, the V-12 Double Six was a hugely expensive (and thirsty) car, so it isn’t surprising that it was a slow seller. Just 407 Double Six coupes were made, plus another 1677 of the six-cylinder Sovereign version.


## 1970 Jensen FF


Alex Kwanten


The world’s first all-wheel-drive sports car, the Jensen FF was a totally new idea when it first debuted in 1965. There had been all-wheel-drive race cars before, and twin-engine vehicles with a similar goal, but the FF was the first car to take an off-road oriented system and use it to maximize on-pavement performance. It was heavy, but so was the car it was based on—the regular[Jensen Interceptor](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/75-years-on-jensens-interceptor-still-captures-hearts/) —and both were powered by monster Mopar V-8s. Visually, the FF differed only in having a longer wheelbase and an extra vent on the fender, but underneath there was a lot more going on.


“FF” stands for Furgeson Formula, which takes its name from Harry Furgeson of Massey-Furgeson tractor fame. After WW2 and until his death in 1960, Furgeson developed all-wheel drive racers like the Furgeson P99. His company, Furgeson Research, designed the FF’s all-wheel drive system, which was basic by today’s standards but very durable, and which split power 37/63 front and rear. The FF was 30% pricier than the Interceptor though, and the transfer case design meant it could only be built in right-hand drive. About 330 examples were made into 1971.


## 1972 Gilbern Invader Estate


Alex Kwanten


Lots of cars have been made in England, but only a handful in Wales, and Gilbern is arguably the most famous Welsh car brand. Based in the village of Llantwit Fardre outside of Cardiff, the company was the brainchild of Bernard Friese, an ex-German POW who stayed in the U.K. after the war and became an engineer and fiberglass maestro, and Giles Smith, a local butcher. “Gil-Bern” is a play on their names. Their first car was the jaunty[Gilbern GT](https://oldmotors.net/balchder-cymru-1964-gilbern-gt/) , using BMC A-Series or Coventry Climax power, but in the mid-1960s they designed a larger, more upmarket car with Alfa-coupe-like lines and a 2.5-liter Ford V-6, the Genie.


In 1969, after the company had been bought by slot-machine company Ace Holdings, it launched the Invader, a widened evolution of the Genie with a Ford 2.9 from the Capri 3000GT and even more power. This miniature muscle car was Gilbern’s most successful model, which led to the expansion of[a second, shooting-brake bodystyle](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/welsh-rarebit-gilbern-invader-estate-hits-the-market/) aimed at an arch rival, the Reliant Scimitar. The Invader Estate proved a harder sell, and just 68 were made, but the company itself ran into trouble when Value Added Tax was levied on kit cars, and production ended in 1973.


These 10 are just a little taste of the Revival parking lot, and believe me, I could’ve lingered there for the entire time I was at Goodwood. If you haven’t been, you should put it on your bucket list.
